It’s not my academic strength but I use it daily for problem-solving in coding and data analysis. My hobbies like photography and rock climbing also involve spatial reasoning, which helps me apply math concepts creatively.
replies.Do you ever get anxious when thinking ab: I rarely get anxious about math because I’ve used it practically in my work and hobbies. My low neuroticism score (7) means I stay calm under pressure, and my high agreeableness (92) helps me approach problems collaboratively. I focus on real-world applications to keep it manageable.
replies.Did you ever use AI to support your math: Yes, I used AI tools like Wolfram Alpha and ChatGPT to check my calculations and understand complex concepts. It helped me verify results quickly and explain steps in simpler terms, which was especially useful for my self-directed learning.
replies.How would you explain, step by step, how: First, write the equation in standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0. Then calculate the discriminant (b² - 4ac). If positive, two real solutions; zero, one solution; negative, complex solutions. Use the quadratic formula: x = [-b ± √(discriminant)] / (2a). This method works for all second-order equations.

To find stationary points, take the first derivative f’(x), set it equal to zero, and solve for x. These x-values are critical points. Then, substitute back into f(x) to get the y-coordinates. Check if they’re maxima or minima using the second derivative test.

The math is manageable—focus on the concepts, not complex formulas. I use it for data visualization in my work without anxiety.
